extracted.intended_audience: colleges and universities (Title IX recipients), Title IX coordinators, institutional legal counsel, policymakers, and commenters on Title IX rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance on what constitutes actionable sexual harassment under Title IX and how institutions must treat complaints, balanced against First Amendment and academic freedom protections on college campuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Davis severe/pervasive/objectively_offensive standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Sexual harassment must be "so severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive that it effectively bars the victim's access to an educational opportunity or benefit." (Davis phrasing including variants expressing denial of access to educational opportunities or benefits.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standard is the threshold for Title IX institutional liability: harassment must be sufficiently severe/pervasive/objectively offensive to deprive victims of access to educational opportunities. The preamble cites multiple formulations from Davis (e.g., "depriv[ing] the victims of access to the educational opportunities or benefits provided by the school," "effectively den[ying] equal access to an institution's resources and opportunities"). Courts apply this objective denial-of-access test when determining actionable harassment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quid_pro_quo_and_Clery/VAWA_offenses_are_per_se
rubrics_metrics.description: Discrete sex offenses and quid pro quo harassment and Clery/VAWA offenses are treated as per se sexual harassment under Title IX because such categories are not entitled to First Amendment protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final regulations return to the Davis definition verbatim while explicitly protecting against even single instances of quid pro quo harassment and Clery/VAWA offenses; these discrete offenses are actionable without meeting the severe/pervasive Davis threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismissal_requirement_for_non-Title_IX_conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §106.45(b)(3)(i), "The recipient must investigate the allegations in a formal complaint. If the conduct alleged ... would not constitute sexual harassment as defined in §106.30 even if proved, did not occur in the recipient's education program or activity, or did not occur against a person in the United States, then the recipient must dismiss the formal complaint with regard to that conduct for purposes of sexual harassment under Title IX or this part; such a dismissal does not preclude action under another provision of the recipient's code of conduct."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural requirement: institutions must dismiss formal Title IX complaints that fall outside the regulatory definition/scope, but nondismissal under Title IX does not bar disciplinary action under other institutional codes or authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: First_Amendment_and_academic_freedom_protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic freedom is protected under the First Amendment; the college classroom is the "marketplace of ideas," and First Amendment principles are crucial in both public and private institutions (with contractual enforcement applicable to private universities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department must interpret and enforce federal laws consistent with the U.S. Constitution; where public universities restrict speech, First Amendment jurisprudence controls, and private universities' promises of free speech may be enforced contractually. Regulations should therefore respect free speech and academic freedom in crafting the definition and enforcement of sexual harassment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content_and_viewpoint_neutrality_narrow_tailoring_clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: School regulations and actions that impact speech must be content and viewpoint neutral and must be narrowly tailored to fit the circumstances; they must be clear enough for a person of ordinary intelligence to understand, or courts will find them unconstitutionally void for vagueness. They cannot overreach by covering both protected and unprotected speech or act as a prior restraint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies that are vague, overbroad, or viewpoint-discriminatory can chill speech and be struck down. Institutions should draft harassment rules narrowly and clearly to avoid constitutional infirmities (citations to Sokolow et al., cases on vagueness/overbreadth/ prior restraint).

rubrics_metrics.name: Not_every_offensive_comment_is_actionable_avoid_general_civility_code
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX (like Title VII) is not to be construed as a federal civility statute; minor annoyances, insults, sporadic teasing, gender-based banter, and occasional abusive language generally do not constitute actionable harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require demanding standards so Title IX/Title VII do not become general civility codes; institutional policies and enforcement should filter out ordinary workplace/student tribulations and focus on conduct meeting the high severity/pervasiveness threshold (see Faragher, Davis, and related commentary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversion_of_severe_verbal_harassment_to_regulable_conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Where harassing speech is severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive enough to create deprivation of equal educational access, courts and regulators may treat that speech as 'verbal conduct' that can be regulated consistent with the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doctrine explains how purely expressive conduct can become regulable when it rises to the level of discriminatory conduct that denies access; parallels exist between Meritor (Title VII) and Davis (Title IX). The regulation of speech must still respect First Amendment limits by applying the Davis threshold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories_of_speech_not_entitled_to_constitutional_protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain kinds of conduct/speech—physical assault, threats of violence, fighting words, and speech whose immediate object is to facilitate criminal conduct—are not entitled to First Amendment protection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited (R.A.V., Wisconsin v. Mitchell, United States v. Osinger) support that where speech is concomitant with special harms (assault, threats, facilitating crimes), it may be regulated or criminalized without raising First Amendment concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional_responses_other_than_discipline_supportive_measures_and_institutional_speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients retain the discretion to respond to offensive student (or employee) speech by providing the complainant with supportive measures, responding with institutional speech, or offering programming designed to foster a welcoming campus climate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble notes these non-punitive tools as ways institutions may address offensive expression without imposing speech-restrictive sanctions; such measures help preserve free-speech principles while supporting affected individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish_discriminatory_harassment_from_generic_harassment_and_consider_cumulative_harms
rubrics_metrics.description: While research and commenters note that repeated microaggressions and small incidents can cumulatively harm targets' mental and physical health, legal standards require discriminatory harassment (severe/pervasive/objectively offensive) rather than treating any 'being bothered' as Title IX harassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-makers and institutions should recognize the difference between cumulative harms described by social science (microaggressions) and the constitutional/legal thresholds for actionable discrimination; avoid conflating generic harassment with discriminatory harassment under Title IX.
